title: Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station
statement: The array `stations` lists the positions of existing gas stations along a straight road (a number line), in strictly increasing order. You must build `k` additional stations, each at any point you choose; positions do not have to be integers. Once they are built, look at the largest gap between two neighbouring stations. Return the smallest value that largest gap can have. Answers within `10^-5` of the exact value are accepted.
constraints: stations is sorted in strictly increasing order
notes:
## Intuition

Handing out the `k` stations one by one, always to the gap whose pieces are currently longest, gives the right answer but costs O(k · n), and `k` can be a million. Flip the question: for a candidate largest gap `D`, how many new stations are needed so that no gap exceeds `D`? A gap of length `g` needs `ceil(g / D) - 1` of them. That count only grows as `D` shrinks, so the smallest `D` whose count fits in `k` can be found by binary search over real numbers.

## Approach

1. Set `low = 0` and `high` to the widest existing gap (with no new stations the answer is at most that).
2. Repeat 100 times: take `mid` halfway between `low` and `high`.
3. Add up `needed`, the stations required for every gap to be at most `mid`.
4. If `needed <= k`, `mid` is achievable, so move `high` down to it; otherwise move `low` up to it.
5. After 100 halvings the interval is far below `10^-5`; return `high`, which is always achievable.

## Example 1, step by step

`stations = [1, ..., 10]` has nine gaps of length 1 and `k = 9`. Start with `low = 0`, `high = 1`. For `mid = 0.5` each gap needs `ceil(1 / 0.5) - 1 = 1` station, so `needed = 9 <= 9` and `high = 0.5`. For `mid = 0.25` each needs 3, so `needed = 27` and `low = 0.25`. Every later `mid` below 0.5 needs at least 18 stations, so `high` stays at `0.5`, the answer.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · 100): each of the 100 rounds scans all gaps once.
- Space: O(1) beyond the input.

## Pitfalls

- A gap of length `g` split into pieces of at most `D` needs `ceil(g / D) - 1` new stations, not `ceil(g / D)`.
- Loop a fixed number of times rather than `while (high - low > eps)`: with positions near `10^8`, a too-small `eps` may never be reached in floating point.
- Return `high`, the side known to be feasible, not `low`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `low`, `high` | bounds on the answer: `low` is too small, `high` is achievable |
| `mid` | the candidate largest gap tested in this round |
| `needed` | new stations required to make every gap at most `mid` |
| `step` | round counter of the binary search |

narration.2: low is a lower bound on the answer; the true answer is above it.
narration.3: high will start as the widest gap, which is achievable even without new stations.
narration.4: Visit each pair of neighbouring stations.
narration.5: Keep the widest gap seen so far.
narration.8: Halve the search interval a fixed number of times; 100 is far more than floating point needs.
narration.9: Try the value halfway between the bounds as the largest allowed gap.
narration.11: Look at every existing gap again.
narration.12: Splitting this gap into pieces no longer than mid takes ceil(gap / mid) - 1 new stations.
narration.14: Can k stations achieve a largest gap of mid?
narration.15: Yes: the answer is at most mid, so pull high down.
narration.17: No: the answer is above mid, so push low up.
narration.20: high is always achievable and now within rounding error of the true minimum.
